topics.title: Headings h1-h6
topics.summary: Six heading levels create the outline of a page for readers, search engines and screen readers.
topics.description:
HTML has six heading elements: `<h1>` (most important, largest) down to `<h6>` (least important, smallest). Headings are not just "big text" - they form the **outline** of your page.

### Why headings matter
- **Readers** scan a page by its headings.
- **Search engines** use them to understand what the page is about.
- **Screen reader users** jump from heading to heading to navigate, so the order must make sense.

### Rules to follow
1. Use **one `<h1>` per page** for the main title (the traditional, safest approach).
2. Go in order: `h1` → `h2` → `h3`. Do not skip levels (e.g. `h1` straight to `h3`) just to get a smaller size.
3. Choose a heading by *meaning*, then control the size with CSS.
4. Do not use headings just to make text bold or big.

### Default look
Browsers give headings a bold weight and a default size (`h1` ≈ 2em, `h2` ≈ 1.5em, `h3` ≈ 1.17em, `h4` = 1em, `h5` ≈ 0.83em, `h6` ≈ 0.67em) plus vertical margins. All of this can be changed with CSS.

### Example outline
```
h1 The Best HTML Course
  h2 Basics
    h3 Tags
    h3 Attributes
  h2 Forms
```
keyPoints: h1 is the most important, h6 the least; six levels in total.
Use a single h1 per page for the main topic.
Do not skip levels; keep a logical hierarchy.
Pick headings for meaning and use CSS for size.
Screen readers and search engines rely on headings.
pitfalls: Skipping from h1 to h4 because you like the font size.
Using <h1> for the logo and again for the page title.
Using <b> or a styled <div> instead of a heading for section titles.

interview.q: How many heading levels exist in HTML?
interview.a: Six: h1 to h6.

interview.q: What happens if you skip heading levels?
interview.a: The page still renders, but the outline becomes confusing for screen reader users and search engines. Keep a proper hierarchy.

interview.q: How many h1 tags should a page have?
interview.a: The traditional best practice is one h1 per page describing the main topic.

interview.q: Should I use headings to make text big?
interview.a: No. Use headings for structure and CSS font-size for visual size.

topics.title: Quotes, Abbreviations, Time & More Inline Semantics
topics.summary: blockquote, q, cite, abbr, time, address, dfn, wbr and other meaningful text elements.
topics.description:
Beyond bold and italic, HTML has small elements that add precise meaning. They help accessibility, SEO and give you hooks for CSS.

### Quotations
- `<blockquote cite="url">` - a long quote set apart as a block.
- `<q>` - a short inline quote; the browser adds quotation marks.
- `<cite>` - the title of a work (book, song, film) being referenced.

### Terms and abbreviations
- `<abbr title="World Health Organization">WHO</abbr>` - shows the full form on hover and tells assistive tech.
- `<dfn>` - the defining instance of a term.

### Dates and times
`<time datetime="2026-10-14">14 Oct 2026</time>` gives machines an exact, machine-readable value while humans see friendly text. Search engines and calendars can use it.

### Contact info
`<address>` marks contact information for the nearest `<article>` or the whole page (author, email, postal address). It is *not* for any random address.

### Other useful inline elements
| Element | Use |
|---|---|
| `<wbr>` | A place where a very long word may break |
| `<bdo dir="rtl">` | Override text direction |
| `<data value="42">` | Machine-readable value for content |
| `<ruby>` | Pronunciation annotations (East Asian text) |

Every one of these is **phrasing content**: it sits inside paragraphs and does not start a new line.
keyPoints: blockquote = block quote, q = inline quote, cite = title of a work.
abbr + title gives the full form of an abbreviation.
time datetime="..." makes dates machine readable.
address is for contact details of the author/page owner.
wbr suggests where long words may wrap.
pitfalls: Using blockquote just to indent text - use CSS margin instead.
Wrapping the quotation marks yourself inside <q> (the browser adds them).
Using <address> for any postal address in the content.

interview.q: Difference between <q> and <blockquote>?
interview.a: q is for short inline quotes and gets automatic quotation marks; blockquote is a block-level element for longer quotations.

interview.q: Why use the <time> element?
interview.a: Its datetime attribute provides a machine-readable date/time so browsers, search engines and assistive tech can understand it.

interview.q: What is <abbr> used for?
interview.a: To mark an abbreviation; the title attribute gives the expansion, shown as a tooltip.

topics.title: HTML Entities (Special Characters)
topics.summary: Use < & © and numeric references to show reserved or hard-to-type characters.
topics.description:
Some characters have a special meaning in HTML (`<` starts a tag, `&` starts an entity). To show them as plain text, or to show characters missing from your keyboard, you use **character entities**. An entity starts with `&` and ends with `;`. ### Common named entities | Entity | Result | Meaning | |---|---|---| | `<` | < | less than | | `>` | > | greater than | | `&` | & | ampersand | | `"` | " | double quote | | `'` | ' | apostrophe | | ` ` | (space) | non-breaking space | | `©` | © | copyright | | `®` | ® | registered | | `™` | ™ | trademark | | `♥` | ♥ | heart | | `€` | € | euro | ### Numeric references Every Unicode character has a number. Use decimal `$` or hexadecimal `$` to display the dollar sign `$`. This works for any character, even without a name. ###   - non-breaking space It is a space that the browser will not collapse and will not wrap at. Good for keeping "10 km" or "Mr. Thapa" on one line. Do **not** use many of them for layout. ### Why they matter - Show HTML code on a page: `<p>` displays as

. - Prevent parsing problems with `&` in URLs and text. - With UTF-8 you can usually type © or € directly, but entities are still needed for `<`, `>` and `&`.
keyPoints: Entities start with & and end with ;.
< > & " are the four you must know.
Numeric references work for any Unicode character: $ or $.

pitfalls: Typing a raw < in text - the browser may treat it as a tag.

topics.title: Ordered & Unordered Lists
topics.summary: ul for bullets, ol for numbered steps, li for each item and the attributes type, start and reversed.
topics.description:
Lists group related items. HTML has three kinds; this topic covers the two most used.

### Unordered list `<ul>`
Items have no order and show bullet points. Use it for menus, features, tags.

### Ordered list `<ol>`
Items where order matters - steps, rankings. Items are numbered automatically.

Each item is an `<li>` (list item). The only valid direct children of `<ul>` / `<ol>` are `<li>` elements.

### Ordered list attributes
| Attribute | Effect |
|---|---|
| `type="1 / A / a / I / i"` | Numbering style |
| `start="10"` | First number |
| `reversed` | Count downwards |
| `<li value="5">` | Force a specific number |

`start`, `type` and `reversed` work **only on `<ol>`**, not on `<ul>`.

### Styling markers with CSS
`list-style-type` accepts `disc`, `circle`, `square`, `none` (for ul) and `decimal`, `lower-alpha`, `upper-alpha`, `lower-roman`, `upper-roman` (for ol).

### Navigation menus
Menus are lists of links. Remove bullets and lay items in a row with CSS:

```css
.menu { list-style: none; display: flex; gap: 10px; }
```

A list-based nav is the standard markup pattern because screen readers announce "list of 4 items".
keyPoints: ul = bullets (no order), ol = numbers (order matters).
Only li elements are direct children of ul/ol.
type, start, reversed work on ol only.
Use CSS list-style-type to change markers.
Navigation menus are semantically lists of links.
pitfalls: Placing text or <div> directly inside <ul> without <li>.

Using
and symbols to fake a list.
Using <ul start="5"> - start is not valid on ul.

interview.q: When do you use ol vs ul?
interview.a: ol when the sequence matters (steps, rankings); ul when it does not (shopping list, menu).

interview.q: What does the start attribute do?
interview.a: On an ol it sets the number of the first item, e.g. start="10" begins at 10. It does not work on ul.

interview.q: How do you build a horizontal navigation menu?
interview.a: Use a ul of li > a links inside nav, then CSS: list-style:none and display:flex (or inline-block on li).

interview.a: Inside an li element of the parent list.
